Motion, once apparently shattered into fragments, is ultimately reassembled through limits, calculation, and patient mathematical abstraction.

text: Literary translation rests on a beautiful contradiction: to remain faithful to a poem, the translator must be unfaithful to its words. If every event, including each firing of a neuron, follows inevitably from prior physical causes, the sense in which we author our choices dissolves. Deliberation itself is a cascade of causes tracing back before our birth; somewhere behind every "I chose" lies a chain we never initiated. Incompatibilists conclude that free will is an illusion.

Compatibilists reply that this argument attacks the wrong target. Freedom never meant exemption from causality—random, uncaused choices would hardly be freer. What matters is that actions flow from the agent's own desires, values, and reasoning rather than coercion or pathology. Harry Frankfurt distinguishes desires we identify with from those we merely suffer; Daniel Dennett emphasizes "elbow room"—the capacity to respond to reasons, imagine alternatives, and regulate our own conduct. On this view, a person deciding after deliberation is free even if that deliberation was determined, because it is genuinely theirs.

Responsibility, compatibilists add, remains coherent: we hold people accountable for acts issuing from their character, and holding them accountable is itself part of the causal fabric shaping future choices. Skeptics retort that this redefines rather than rescues freedom. Perhaps. But if free will survives at all, it may be this: not escaping the causal order, but acting meaningfully within it.
